analysis.one_liner: Strips Wisconsin tribes of treaty rights to hunt, fish, and gather off their reservations.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote, leaving the treaty rights it targeted intact.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cancel, by act of Congress, every off-reservation right of federally recognized tribes to hunt, fish, and gather anywhere in Wisconsin — including rights that federal courts had confirmed in the tribes' ceded territory [S2] [S3]. It was aimed squarely at the treaty rights that allowed Ojibwe tribal members to fish and hunt outside reservation boundaries, a flashpoint in northern Wisconsin in the 1980s when courts sided with the tribes and non-Indian anglers protested. No tribe, business, or constituent appears to have formally backed it: it drew no cosponsors and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Non-Indian anglers and hunters in northern Wisconsin, who would no longer face the court-ordered catch limits or spring tribal spearing they blamed for smaller daily bag limits; the sport-fishing and tourism businesses that serve them; and the state, which would regain sole control over fish and wildlife outside reservations [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Northern Wisconsin anglers and tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: Wipes out every off-reservation hunting, fishing, and gathering right held by any federally recognized tribe in Wisconsin — whether it came from a treaty, a law, an executive order, or a federal court order — erasing the rights the tribes won in litigation.

Would end the court-ordered allocation system under which tribal members spear walleye in the spring, before the general angling season, removing the limits on non-Indian anglers' catch that were the bill's real-world grievance.
Returns full regulatory control over fish and wildlife outside reservation lands to the state, rather than the shared federal-court-supervised system then in place.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Wisconsin's Ojibwe tribes, who would lose treaty-guaranteed hunting, fishing, and gathering rights that federal courts had affirmed — rights their families use for food and income. Beyond Wisconsin, every U.S. treaty promise would be worth less, since Congress would have shown it can cancel a treaty obligation by simple statute.

drawbacks.text: The rights the bill cancels are not privileges — the tribes ceded millions of acres of land in exchange for guarantees to keep hunting and fishing on it, and federal courts found those guarantees still binding. Wiping them out by statute would leave the tribes having sold their land and received nothing in return.
Tribal families would lose a source of food and income, since the off-reservation harvest the bill abolishes is a treaty-based livelihood, not a special exemption.

The bill goes far beyond even its supporters' stated grievance. Anglers' complaint was about spring spearing and court-ordered bag limits, but the bill abolishes all off-reservation rights — including gathering and hunting that never affected anyone's fishing — and nullifies court orders by flat statute, which would invite years of litigation and deepen rather than settle the conflict.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are modest and one-sided: non-Indian anglers would get somewhat larger bag limits and no spring spearing to share the water with, and tourism operators would see fewer boat-landing confrontations. Against that, a small tribal community would permanently lose treaty rights protecting its food supply and livelihood, and the United States would undermine the binding force of its own treaties everywhere. The costs clearly outweigh the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Interior Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative F. James Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on April 18, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs — the committee that handles Indian affairs legislation.
That referral was the bill's last recorded action. No hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever took place.
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor — the bill stood alone from introduction to death.

The bill existed because federal courts had ruled for the tribes: the text abrogates rights 'granted by any treaty, law, Executive order, or Federal court order,' a direct legislative response to the court rulings confirming Ojibwe off-reservation harvest rights in Wisconsin's ceded territory.
When the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, the bill died with it, and the treaty rights it targeted were never touched.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wisconsin's tribal nations came out ahead: their treaty-affirmed off-reservation hunting, fishing, and gathering rights survived untouched because the bill never advanced. The committee that let it sit also avoided a divisive floor fight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wisconsin tribes, whose treaty rights survived

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred, so party positions were never recorded; the only measurable support was one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.industry: Tribal (Ojibwe) commercial and subsistence fishing and hunting
industries.note: The bill would abolish the treaty-based harvest that supplies food and income to tribal families in Wisconsin's ceded territory. These are ordinary working people exercising rights courts had already confirmed; the bill's cost would fall directly on them.

industries.industry: Sport fishing and tourism in northern Wisconsin
industries.note: Court orders in the ceded territory allocated fish so tribal spearers took walleye before the general season and non-Indian anglers faced reduced limits. Abrogating the tribal rights would hand that catch to sport anglers and the lodges, guides, and bait shops that serve them — a gain bought directly by extinguishing another community's treaty rights.

The bill would end the court-supervised sharing of fish and wildlife authority with the tribes and restore sole state regulatory control outside reservations. That is institutional power, not a gain or loss for citizens directly.
